stages.title: Intermediate vocabulary
stages.hook: Why do "embarazada" and "embarrassed" look alike but mean different things?
explain: Intermediate vocabulary grows through word families and cognates. Many Spanish words resemble English because both come from Latin: "importante", "familia", "información". But there are false friends: "embarazada" means pregnant, "éxito" means success, "actual" means current, and "librería" is a bookshop.

Suffixes build new words: -ero for people (zapato, zapatero), -ción for nouns (informar, información), -mente for adverbs (rápido, rápidamente). Prefixes such as des- give the opposite: hacer, deshacer.
stages.mnemonic: Cognates are friends, false friends are tricksters.

gq.q: What is the opposite of "hacer" with des-?
gq.why: Des- often forms the opposite: deshacer means to undo.

panel.q: Which word is a false friend?
panel.why: Éxito looks like exit but means success.

panel.q: How does Spanish form many adverbs from adjectives?
panel.why: Rápida + mente gives rápidamente.

panel.q: Why are cognates useful and what is the risk?
panel.model: They help you guess words quickly because the languages share Latin roots, but false friends may mean something different.
panel.why: Cognates and false cognates.

teach.model: Many Spanish words look like English words because both use Latin roots. Check false friends, which look the same but differ in meaning. Learn suffixes like -mente and prefixes like des-.

points.ask: How do I make new words?

stages.title: Verb forms and time expressions
stages.hook: "Ayer comí" and "Cuando era niño comía": why two past tenses?
explain: The preterite (pretérito indefinido) tells finished events: "Ayer hablé con ella." The imperfect describes habits and background in the past: "Cuando era niño, jugaba en la calle." For a one-time event within a scene, combine both: "Estaba lloviendo cuando salí."

Future: "voy a comer" (near future with ir a) or "comeré" (simple future). Present perfect: "he comido". Time words: ayer, anoche, la semana pasada (preterite); siempre, todos los días, a menudo (imperfect).
stages.mnemonic: Preterite = a snapshot; imperfect = a film.
sentences: Yesterday I ate with my friends.
As a child I played outside.
Tomorrow I am going to travel.

gq.q: Which tense fits "Todos los veranos íbamos a la playa"?
gq.why: A repeated habit in the past uses the imperfect.

gq.q: How do you say "I am going to study"?
gq.why: Near future: ir a plus the infinitive.

panel.q: "Hablé" vs "hablaba": which stresses a completed action?
panel.why: The preterite presents the action as completed.

panel.q: In "Leía cuando sonó el teléfono", which action is the background?
panel.why: The imperfect gives the ongoing background and the preterite interrupts it.

panel.q: When would you use the imperfect rather than the preterite?
panel.model: The imperfect describes habits, ongoing actions and background in the past without a defined end.
panel.why: Aspect distinction.

teach.model: Use the preterite for finished events, like ayer comí. Use the imperfect for habits and descriptions, like comía todos los días. For future use ir a plus the infinitive.

points.ask: When do I use the preterite?
When do I use the imperfect?
How do I talk about the future?

stages.title: Complex sentence introduction
stages.hook: How do you say "I think that it is true" or "I stayed home because it rained"?
explain: Complex sentences use connectors. "Que" joins clauses: "Creo que es verdad." "Porque" gives a reason, "aunque" shows contrast, "cuando" gives time, "si" gives a condition: "Si llueve, me quedo en casa."
Relative clauses use que: "El libro que leí es largo." "Donde" and "quien" are also used: "La persona con quien hablé es mi tía." Use a comma after an opening clause: "Aunque estaba cansado, salí."
stages.mnemonic: Que is the glue of Spanish.
sentences: I think that it is true.
If it rains, I stay home.
Although I was tired, I went out.

gq.why: Que introduces a relative clause about things.

panel.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: Creo que tú tienes razón de.
panel.why: Creer que joins the main clause and the next one; the English "that" can sometimes be left out but que cannot.

panel.q: Why is the que never omitted in Spanish, unlike "that" in English?
o: Spanish clauses need que to be joined
panel.why: In English you can say "I think it is true"; in Spanish you must say "Creo que es verdad".

panel.q: Explain the difference between "porque" and "aunque".
panel.model: Porque gives a reason (because), whereas aunque expresses contrast (although).
panel.why: Connectors.

teach.model: Use que to join two clauses, as in creo que es verdad. Use porque for reasons, aunque for contrast, cuando for time and si for conditions. Que cannot be dropped, unlike that in English.

stages.title: Reading short stories
stages.hook: A story starts: "Había una vez un pueblo sin agua." What do you expect next?
explain: Many Spanish stories begin with "Había una vez..." (once upon a time). Stories use the imperfect for the setting and the preterite for events: "Era de noche. Un niño salió de casa." Look for characters, setting, problem and solution.

Short stories from the Spanish-speaking world include fables and tales by authors from Spain, Mexico, Argentina and elsewhere. Use context to guess unknown words and look for cognates. Read once for the gist, then again for details. Pay attention to dialogue marked with a raya (—): —Hola —dijo.
stages.mnemonic: Había una vez: the doorway into the story.
sentences: Once upon a time there was a village.

gq.q: Which tense usually describes the setting of a story?
gq.why: Era de noche sets the scene in the imperfect.

gq.q: What does the dash (raya) mark in Spanish writing?
gq.why: Spanish often uses a raya to introduce a speaker's words.

panel.q: In "Era de noche cuando llegó", which verb is the event?
panel.why: The preterite llegó is the event.

panel.q: How can you work out a word you do not know?
panel.model: Use the context and look for cognates or word parts to guess its meaning.
panel.why: Reading strategy.

panel.q: Why does the story say "había" and not "hubo" in "Había una vez"?
o: It describes a setting, so the imperfect is used
panel.why: Había introduces the background of the tale.

teach.model: Look for who, where and what the problem is. The setting is in the imperfect and the events are in the preterite. Use cognates and context to guess words. Notice the dash that marks dialogue.

points.ask: How do I deal with new words?

stages.title: Listening comprehension
stages.hook: On a metro loudspeaker in Madrid: "Próxima estación: Sol." What do you listen for?
explain: To follow Spanish, listen for key words and numbers. Spanish speakers often link words: "los otros" can sound like "lo-so-tros". Final s may fade in some Caribbean dialects: "los amigos" sounds like "loh amigo".

Strategies: predict from the situation, listen for question words, note the time, place and number. In announcements, expect fixed phrases: "Atención, por favor", "El tren con destino a..." Replay the audio and focus on one detail each time.
stages.mnemonic: Gist first, then numbers, names and times.

gq.q: What should you listen for first?
In some Caribbean dialects "los amigos" can sound like "loh amigo". What is this?
o: Adding a letter at the end of words

panel.q: How do you say "ticket" in Spain and in much of Latin America?
panel.why: Word choice varies: billete in Spain, boleto in Mexico and elsewhere, pasaje in some countries.

panel.q: Why is it harder to hear separate words in Spanish speech?
panel.model: Spanish speakers link words and blend vowels together, so word boundaries are not always clear.
panel.why: Resyllabification.

panel.q: Which is the best strategy for a station announcement?
o: Listen for place names, times and numbers
panel.why: Key details matter most in announcements.

teach.model: Listen first for the main idea. Then listen again for numbers, names and times. Words are linked in speech so they can sound joined. Accents differ from place to place.

stages.title: Conversation and pronunciation
stages.hook: Why does "perro" have a rolled r but "pero" a tap? Can the difference change meaning?
explain: Spanish has two r sounds. A single r between vowels is a quick tap: "pero" (but). Double rr and r at the start of a word are rolled: "perro" (dog), "rojo". The difference changes meaning: pero versus perro.

The letter j (and g before e or i) is a throaty /x/ sound: "jugar", "gente". The letter ll and y vary by region. In much of Latin America and parts of Spain "c" before e or i and "z" sound like "s" (seseo), while in most of Spain they sound like English "th" (distinción). Intonation: questions rise at the end.
stages.mnemonic: Pero (tap) is but, perro (roll) is dog.

gq.q: Which word has a rolled r?
gq.why: Double rr makes the rolled sound.

o: like g in "go", as in English
gq.why: G before e or i is /x/.

panel.q: What is "seseo"?
o: Pronouncing z and c before e/i as s
Rolling the r at the start of every word
panel.why: It is the usual pronunciation in Latin America and southern Spain.

panel.q: "Caro" and "carro" differ because...
o: one has a tap and the other a roll
they are different spellings of the same word
panel.why: The different r sounds make different words.

panel.q: Why is it important to pronounce rr differently from r?
panel.model: The two sounds distinguish words, such as pero (but) and perro (dog).
panel.why: Phonemic contrast.

teach.model: Spanish has a tap r and a rolled rr. They make different words. The letter j and g before e or i sound like a throaty h. In many places z and c before e or i sound like s.

points.ask: How many r sounds are there?
How do j and g sound?

stages.title: Writing paragraphs
stages.hook: How can three sentences become a clear paragraph in Spanish?
explain: A paragraph (párrafo) starts with a main idea sentence, adds details, and ends with a conclusion. Linking words (conectores) help: primero, luego, además, sin embargo, por eso, finalmente. Use a capital letter only at the start of a sentence and for names.

Be careful with spelling. Remember accent marks, the ¿ and ¡ marks, and the difference between "haber" (there is) and "a ver" (let's see). Common errors: "hay/ay/ahí", "porque/porqué/por qué". Read your paragraph aloud and check that verbs agree with their subjects.
stages.mnemonic: Idea, details, finish: a paragraph is a little essay.

gq.q: Which is correct: "There is a book on the table"?
o: Hay un libro en la mesa.
Ay un libro en la mesa.
Ahí un libro en la mesa.
Hay un libro a la mesa.
gq.why: Hay is a form of haber; ay and ahí are different words.

panel.q: Which sentence uses the right word?
panel.why: Ver means to see (a ver is a different phrase, let's see); haber is another verb, used for there is and for compound tenses.

panel.q: Why are ¡ and ¿ used?
o: They mark the start of an exclamation or question
panel.why: Spanish marks both ends of questions and exclamations.

panel.q: How do linking words improve a paragraph?
panel.model: They connect ideas and show how sentences relate, so the paragraph is clear and flows logically.
panel.why: Cohesion.

teach.model: Start with the main idea. Add two or three details. Use linking words like primero and sin embargo. Finish with a closing sentence. Check accents and punctuation.

stages.title: Cultural expressions and idioms
stages.hook: If someone says "Estoy en las nubes", should you look up at the sky?
explain: Idioms carry meaning beyond words: "estar en las nubes" means to be daydreaming, "costar un ojo de la cara" means to cost a fortune, "meter la pata" means to make a blunder, "ser pan comido" means to be very easy. Many sayings (refranes) express traditional wisdom: "Más vale tarde que nunca" (better late than never).

Culture shows in expressions: "sobremesa" is the time spent chatting at the table after a meal. Gestures and greetings differ: a kiss on the cheek is common in Spain and many Latin American countries. Idioms vary by country, so some are used in Mexico but not in Spain.
stages.mnemonic: Picture the idiom: la pata en el barro!
items: costar un ojo de la cara
to be in a very good mood

o: to put on your shoes quickly
gq.why: It is an idiom for a mistake.

o: Time chatting at the table after eating
gq.why: It is a cultural practice of lingering at the table.

panel.q: Why is a literal translation of "ser pan comido" misleading?
panel.why: Idioms must be understood as units.

panel.q: Why do idioms differ between Spanish-speaking countries?
panel.model: Each region has its own history and culture, so expressions develop differently and are not always shared.
panel.why: Regional variation.

panel.q: A friend says "Estoy en las nubes". What are they doing?
panel.why: It describes being absent-minded.

teach.model: An idiom is a fixed phrase with a special meaning. Do not translate it word for word. Estar en las nubes means to daydream. Customs like the sobremesa and greeting with a kiss differ from place to place.

stages.title: Practical travel communication
stages.hook: You arrive at a Spanish airport. Which phrases will you need first?
explain: Travel phrases: "¿Dónde está la salida?" "Un billete a Sevilla, por favor." "¿A qué hora sale el tren?" "Necesito una habitación." Use "perdone" or "disculpe" to get attention. Directions: a la derecha (right), a la izquierda (left), todo recto (straight on).

In hotels: "Tengo una reserva a nombre de...". In restaurants: "La cuenta, por favor". In emergencies: "¡Ayuda!" or "Necesito un médico". Remember travel words vary: "autobús" in Spain, "camión" in Mexico, "guagua" in Cuba and the Canary Islands.
items: At what time does it leave?
sentences: Excuse me, where is the station?

gq.why: It is used for going straight ahead.

gq.q: How would you politely get a stranger's attention?

panel.q: A bus is "autobús" in Spain. What is it in Cuba?
panel.why: Guagua is used in Cuba and the Canary Islands; camión in Mexico; colectivo in Argentina.

panel.q: Which is correct for "I need a room for two nights"?
o: Necesito una habitación para dos noches.
Necesito un habitación por dos noche.
panel.why: Habitación is feminine and plural noches agrees.

panel.q: Why should a traveller learn a few polite phrases in the local language?
panel.model: Polite phrases show respect, and locals respond more warmly, which makes communication and help easier.
panel.why: Intercultural courtesy.

teach.model: Use perdone to get attention. Ask ¿Dónde está...? for places. Learn right, left and straight on: derecha, izquierda, todo recto. Words for bus and ticket vary by country.

points.ask: How do I get attention politely?
How do I ask for a place?
